passages.text: Therefore, before everything else, one ought to know that one finds it nowhere except from a prophet of truth. A true prophet is one who always knows everything, including the thoughts of everyone, and is sinless, as one fully assured concerning God’s judgment. Therefore, we ought not to consider his foreknowledge superficially, but to ask whether his foreknowledge can subsist without any other basis. For physicians foretell things while having the sick person’s pulse as material laid before them; some do so by means of birds, others by means of sacrificial victims, and still others foretell while having many other different materials laid before them—and they are not prophets.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun’s antecedent lies outside the supplied passage; “it” preserves the unresolved reference, probably to truth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a prophet of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the source’s genitive expression rather than replacing it with the interpretive “true prophet,” which appears explicitly in the next sentence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as one fully assured concerning God’s judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πεπληροφορημένος denotes being fully convinced or assured; “fully informed concerning God’s judgment” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: without any other basis
lexical_decisions.rationale: In context πρόφασις denotes an external ground, occasion, or means on which prediction depends; “pretext” is the more usual alternative in other contexts.

lexical_decisions.chosen: material laid before them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase presents the pulse and divinatory objects as supplied material underlying the predictions.

passages.text: But if someone should wish to say that foreknowledge by way of such predictions is similar to genuinely innate foreknowledge, that person is greatly deceived. For things of this kind disclose only what is present, and that only if they prove true. Yet in another respect even these are useful to me, for they establish that foreknowledge exists. But the foreknowledge of the one true prophet not only knows what is present but extends its prophecy without limit as far as the coming age itself, and it needs nothing for understanding—and, of prophecies, dim and ambiguous things, so that what is said should need another prophet for understanding, but explicit and plain things—just as our teacher, being also a prophet, always knew everything by an innate and ever-flowing spirit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: foreknowledge by way of such predictions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The article points to an implied feminine noun, most naturally πρόγνωσις from the immediate context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄλλως δέ μοι καὶ αὐτὰ εὐχρηστεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet in another respect even these are useful to me
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄλλως marks a different respect in which the practices support the author’s argument despite not constituting true prophecy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ δὲ τοῦ μόνου καὶ ἀληθοῦς πρόγνωσις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the foreknowledge of the one true prophet
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Prophet” is supplied from the immediate context after the substantival “the only and true one.” A more formally literal alternative is “the foreknowledge of the only and true one.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μέχρις αὐτοῦ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος ἀπέραντον ἐκτείνει τὴν προφητείαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: extends its prophecy without limit as far as the coming age itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπέραντον characterizes the prophecy as unlimited, while μέχρις states its reach as far as the coming age.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ προφητειῶν ἀμαυρὰ καὶ ἀμφίβολα, ἵνα ἄλλου προφήτου χρείαν ἔχῃ τὰ λεγόμενα πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν, ἀλλὰ ῥητὰ καὶ ἁπλᾶ
lexical_decisions.chosen: and, of prophecies, dim and ambiguous things, so that what is said should need another prophet for understanding, but explicit and plain things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English preserves the printed genitive προφητειῶν, the substantival neuter forms, the purpose clause, and the contrast without silently supplying a missing predicate or extending a negation beyond what the printed syntax securely supports. The resulting fracture reflects an unresolved source construction rather than a settled interpretation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by an innate and ever-flowing spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀένναος can describe something perpetually flowing, unfailing, or unceasing; “by an innate and unceasing spirit” is also possible.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὐδενὸς δεῖται πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν, καὶ προφητειῶν ἀμαυρὰ καὶ ἀμφίβολα, ἵνα ἄλλου προφήτου χρείαν ἔχῃ τὰ λεγόμενα πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν, ἀλλὰ ῥητὰ καὶ ἁπλᾶ
source_issues.issue: The image-checked selected reading is verified as printed, but no defensible continuous syntax can presently be established. προφητειῶν is genitive plural, whereas ἀμαυρὰ καὶ ἀμφίβολα and ῥητὰ καὶ ἁπλᾶ are morphologically nominative/accusative neuter plurals; their precise case and syntactic function cannot be determined from morphology alone. The preceding οὐδενὸς is governed naturally by δεῖται, but it does not securely provide either a predicate for the following neuter forms or the negative contrast apparently expected before ἀλλὰ. The context suggests a contrast between obscure predictions requiring interpretation and explicit, plain predictions, but recovering that meaning requires wording or syntax not securely present in the selected reading. The translation therefore preserves the fracture, and the unresolved construction blocks publication.
source_issues.proposed_reading: One possible but unverified conjecture is καὶ οὐ προφητεύει ἀμαυρὰ καὶ ἀμφίβολα, ἵνα ἄλλου προφήτου χρείαν ἔχῃ τὰ λεγόμενα πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν, ἀλλὰ ῥητὰ καὶ ἁπλᾶ (“and it does not prophesy dim and ambiguous things, so that what is said needs another prophet for understanding, but explicit and plain things”). This conjecture alters and supplements the selected reading and has not been substituted into the translation.

passages.text: Therefore, he confidently gave an account of what was going to happen—I mean sufferings, places, and limits. For, being an unerring prophet, surveying everything with the boundless eye of the soul, he knows it all while himself escaping notice. But if we too admit, as most people do, that even the true prophet has foreknowledge not always but only at times—when he has the spirit and, for that reason, foreknows, but when he does not have it, is ignorant—if we suppose this, we will both deceive ourselves and lay snares for others. For such a thing belongs to those madly inspired by a spirit of disorder, those becoming drunk beside altars and being filled with the reek of burnt fat.

lexical_decisions.chosen: sufferings, places, and limits
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὅροι can denote boundaries, limits, or termini; “limits” preserves the term without conflating it with the explicitly named times in 3.15.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the boundless eye of the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the singular eye image and ἄπειρος in its sense of boundless or unlimited.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he knows it all while himself escaping notice
lexical_decisions.rationale: λανθάνων most naturally describes the prophet as remaining unnoticed while knowing; “he knows secretly” is a possible but less formally precise alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: lay snares for others
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνεδρεύω denotes lying in wait for or entrapping someone, not merely leading someone into an intellectual error.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being filled with the reek of burnt fat
lexical_decisions.rationale: κνίσα is the smoke, steam, or odor of sacrificial fat; “being filled with sacrificial fumes” is a less vivid alternative.

passages.text: For if someone wishing to profess prophecy is allowed to be believed, in the matters in which he is caught as a liar, that at that time he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge, he will not be easy to expose, though he is a prophet who is a liar. For in the cases where, while saying many things, he hits upon a few, he is then believed to have the spirit. Moreover, he speaks of first things as last and last things as first, things that have happened as things that will happen, and things that will happen as though they had already happened. He also says other, incoherent things, things stolen from others and transformed, and some things curtailed, shapeless, senseless, ambiguous, crooked, and unclear, all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ τῆς προγνώσεως ἅγιον οὐκ εἶχεν πνεῦμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s attributive relation between the holy spirit and foreknowledge without imposing a later doctrinal identification.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while saying many things, he hits upon a few
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιτυγχάνει describes occasionally hitting the mark or obtaining a correct result among numerous claims.

lexical_decisions.chosen: things stolen from others
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφαιρέω can mean taking something away secretly; “appropriated from others” is a less pointed alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: curtailed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive describes things reduced, diminished, or mutilated; “curtailed” fits the treatment of allegedly defective predictions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shapeless
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed spelling supports ἀνειδής, “without form, shapeless, unsightly,” rather than ἀναιδής, “shameless.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience
lexical_decisions.rationale: κεκραγότα vividly portrays the statements as openly betraying or proclaiming something; δυσσυνειδησία can denote a bad or guilty conscience and, by extension, unscrupulousness.

passages.text: But our teacher resorted to no such trickery. Rather, as I said earlier, being a prophet who always knew everything by an innate and ever-flowing spirit, he confidently set things out, clearly foretelling sufferings, places, fixed times, ways, and limits. For example, when foretelling about the sanctuary, he said, “Do you see these buildings? Amen, I tell you, not one stone upon another will be left here that will not be torn down,” and, “This generation will certainly not pass away, and the demolition will have its beginning. For they will come and encamp here and throw up an encircling stockade and slaughter your children here.” Likewise, he spoke what follows in a clear voice, things that we are able to see with our own eyes, so that, in the matters about which the word was spoken, the deed might also occur. For the prophet of truth frames the statement of proof to produce faith in those who hear.

lexical_decisions.chosen: resorted to no such trickery
lexical_decisions.rationale: γοητεύω can denote practicing sorcery, bewitching, or deceiving as a charlatan; “trickery” preserves the polemical accusation without requiring a claim of literal magic.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by an innate and ever-flowing spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same expression as in 3.12, apart from the printed spelling ἐμφύτῳ, is rendered consistently; “by an innate and unceasing spirit” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fixed times
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective describes times set or bounded in advance; “appointed times” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: about the sanctuary
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἁγίασμα denotes a holy place or sanctuary; “temple” would make the contextual identification more explicit than the source does.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Amen, I tell you
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the distinctive introductory formula rather than replacing it with the familiar interpretive rendering “Truly, I tell you.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: encamp here
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future form conveys sitting or settling down; in the military context, “encamp” is natural, while “sit down here” is the more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: throw up an encircling stockade
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes enclosing with a palisade or stockade. The Greek supplies no explicit object, so the English likewise avoids specifying whom or what is enclosed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Likewise
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb can mean “equally” or “all the same.” “Nevertheless” is possible, but continuation by similarity best fits the immediate context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα ἐφ᾽ ὧν ὁ λόγος ἐρρέθη, καὶ τὸ ἔργον γένηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that, in the matters about which the word was spoken, the deed might also occur
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ἐφ᾽ ὧν as neuter and topical, referring to the matters about which the statement was made. If ὧν is understood personally and interpreted temporally from the generational context, an alternative is “so that the deed too might occur in the days of those in whose days the word was spoken.” The topical reading avoids supplying an unexpressed noun meaning “days,” while the personal-temporal alternative remains contextually possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς γὰρ πίστιν ἀκουόντων τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀποδείξεως ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας ποιεῖται προφήτης
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the prophet of truth frames the statement of proof to produce faith in those who hear
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγον ποιεῖσθαι can mean formulating or delivering an account, while πρὸς πίστιν states its intended effect. “Gives an account of the demonstration for the faith of the hearers” is a more formal alternative.
